name: Māori Aotearoa
summary: The Polynesian people of Aotearoa (New Zealand), descended from voyagers who arrived around 1320–1350. Over centuries they developed a distinct culture; the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) began British rule.

location.value: Mainland New Zealand (Aotearoa); some later moved to the Chatham Islands (Moriori).

terrain.value: Mountains, volcanic plateaus, dense forests and long coasts on two main islands.
terrain.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

climate.value: Temperate and cooler than tropical Polynesia.
climate.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

resources.value: Kūmara (sweet potato), fish and shellfish, birds (including the moa until it died out), and pounamu (greenstone).
resources.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

disasters.value: Volcanic eruptions (such as Tarawera, 1886) and earthquakes.
disasters.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

population.value: About 100,000 in the late 1700s according to Cook; Michael King suggested about 110,000.

urbanisation.value: Fortified hilltop villages (pā), some very large, and open villages (kāinga).
urbanisation.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

disease.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

migration.value: Arrived in waves of canoe voyages between about 1320 and 1350.

economicBase.value: Hunting, fishing and gathering; the early diet included moa, other large birds and fur seals. Pounamu (greenstone) was used for tools and ornaments. Growing kūmara is not mentioned in the part read.

tradeRoutes.value: Pounamu from the South Island and obsidian were traded across both islands.
tradeRoutes.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

moneyAndTax.value: No money; gifts and exchange between kin groups.
moneyAndTax.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

inequality.value: Chiefs (rangatira) and commoners; captives taken in war became slaves.
inequality.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

governmentType.value: Villages of related families formed hapū (clans or sub-tribes); iwi were the largest social unit. Society had rangatira (chiefs), commoners and slaves, and iwi are usually governed by rūnanga (councils).

keyRulers.value: Rangatira (chiefs) led hapū and iwi. The part of the page read names no individual chiefs, so Hongi Hika and Te Rauparaha remain unchecked.

succession.value: Leadership passed through genealogy (whakapapa), usually to senior lines, but ability mattered too.
succession.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

institutions.value: Tapu (sacredness) and mana (authority and prestige) governed social life.
institutions.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

stability.value: The Musket Wars (about 1807–1842) between iwi killed thousands after muskets arrived.
stability.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

eliteConflict.value: Warfare between iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes) over land and honour.
eliteConflict.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

armyAndTech.value: Taiaha and mere weapons; pā fortifications.
armyAndTech.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

majorWars.value: The Musket Wars, a period of bloody intertribal warfare after muskets arrived; and the New Zealand Wars, after disputed land purchases in the 1860s, with land confiscated as punishment.

territoryChange.value: Lost most land after 1840 through sales, confiscation and wars.
territoryChange.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

alliancesRivals.value: Iwi allied and fought with each other; some fought on the Crown’s side in the New Zealand Wars.
alliancesRivals.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

inventions.value: Developed crafts independently of other Polynesians.

scienceEducation.value: Knowledge passed on orally in houses of learning (whare wānanga), including navigation and genealogy.
scienceEducation.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

communicationTransport.value: Waka (canoes) on rivers, lakes and the sea; walking tracks over mountain passes to reach pounamu.

religion.value: Traditional beliefs such as tapu, mana and wairua, with many deities. In 2018, 7.7% of Māori followed Māori religions, 29.9% Christian denominations and 53.5% no religion; Rātana and Ringatū are Māori Christian groups.

languageWriting.value: Te reo Māori, an oral language until missionaries wrote it in the Latin alphabet (1810s–20s).
languageWriting.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

artsArchitecture.value: Carved meeting houses (wharenui), tā moko (tattoo), weaving and the haka.
artsArchitecture.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

socialStructure.value: Rangatira (chiefs), commoners and slaves, within whānau, hapū and iwi.
socialStructure.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

sharedIdentity.value: Identity based on whakapapa (genealogy) linking people to ancestors, canoes and land.
sharedIdentity.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

dailyLife.value: Whare (houses) of wood and raupō reeds; kūmara, fern root, fish and birds; cooking in earth ovens (hāngī).

neighbours.value: The Moriori of the Chatham Islands; later European and American traders and settlers.
neighbours.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread through missions from 1814; the Kīngitanga (King Movement) began in 1858.
ideasReligions.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

colonisation.value: The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) between the British Crown and Māori chiefs; its meaning is still debated.

peakPeriod.value: Before European contact (14th–18th centuries), as Māori culture developed independently across Aotearoa.
peakPeriod.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

declineSignals.value: Colonisation, land loss and disease reduced the population to about 42,000 by 1896.
declineSignals.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

outcome.value: Māori culture continues today; about 900,000 people identify as Māori.
outcome.source: King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

sources.value: Oral tradition. Checked against Wikipedia (“Māori people”).
